analysis.one_liner: Gives the SEC tougher penalties against securities fraudsters and clamps down on penny stock scams.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on July 23, 1990, three days after it was introduced, but never voted on the Senate's nearly identical version, and the 101st Congress ended without the bill becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the SEC's enforcement toolkit across four securities laws: letting it fine violators up to the greater of $100,000 (individuals) or $500,000 (firms) or the amount of the fraud gain, bar crooked executives from serving as officers or directors, and issue stop-it-now orders that freeze assets in emergencies. It also targets the penny stock market specifically, where boiler-room brokers routinely fleece small investors: brokers would have to give customers a plain-language risk disclosure, reveal their commissions, tell them their stock's market value monthly, and support a national price-quotation system so buyers could actually see what these thinly traded shares are worth. A toll-free hotline for checking broker disciplinary records was also included.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy stocks, especially the small retail investors who were the main victims of penny stock fraud - penny stocks trade for under a few dollars and were a favorite vehicle of boiler-room scams. Honest brokers would also benefit because a more credible market improves their standing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small investors, especially penny stock buyers

how_it_helps.text: Lets the SEC seek civil fines in court of up to the greater of $100,000 for individuals or $500,000 for companies per violation, or the fraudster's gain - penalties the law previously did not allow outside insider-trading cases.
Lets courts bar people who commit securities fraud from serving as corporate officers or directors if they show 'substantial unfitness' to serve.
Gives the SEC authority to issue cease-and-desist orders - including emergency temporary orders that can freeze assets or stop an ongoing scheme before investigators finish their case.
Requires penny stock brokers to hand buyers a written risk disclosure and disclose their commissions, and to send monthly statements showing the market value of the customer's penny stock holdings.
Directs the SEC to set up automated quotation systems so penny stock buyers can see real bid and ask prices instead of relying solely on the broker's word.
Creates a toll-free hotline investors can call to check a broker's disciplinary history.
Restricts 'blank check' shell companies that raise money from investors with no stated business plan, a common penny stock fraud vehicle.
Bars people already sanctioned by the SEC from working around the ban by acting as 'promoters' or 'consultants' in penny stock deals, closing a known loophole.

analysis.who_pays: Fraudulent brokers, penny stock promoters, and securities violators, who would face fines, asset disgorgement, stop orders, and industry bans. Legitimate broker-dealers in the penny stock market would bear compliance costs - mandatory disclosures, monthly customer statements, and quotation-system participation.

drawbacks.text: New disclosure and reporting duties fall on legitimate small broker-dealers, not just scammers, raising their compliance costs and possibly pushing some small firms out of the penny stock business.

The bill gives the SEC new powers to fine people administratively and to issue orders with only temporary-order speed; critics of expanded SEC power worry about due-process limits, though the text does include hearing rights and judicial review.

Mandating an automated quotation system for thousands of thinly traded stocks is an expensive technology buildout with uncertain industry participation, and the bill only 'facilitates' it rather than guaranteeing results.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for investors are concrete and targeted at a documented fraud problem, while the costs - compliance expenses for honest brokerages and a heavier enforcement hand - are real but modest relative to the investor losses the bill targets. The bill's most meaningful protections (disclosure, price transparency, executive bans, real fines) come at little cost to anyone not committing fraud.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote just three days after introduction, then immediately set it aside in favor of a nearly identical Senate bill (S. 647), and neither became law before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 20, 1990 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Just three days later, on July 23, the House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure (suspension of the rules) normally reserved for noncontroversial bills.
The same day, the House laid its own bill on the table and took up S. 647, a similar Senate measure, instead - meaning H.R. 5325 itself was immediately set aside in favor of the companion bill.
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill never became law in this form.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors did not get these protections from this bill in this Congress, so the brokers and promoters who profit from opaque penny stock practices were left untouched a while longer. However, the swift House passage and the existence of an identical Senate companion bill suggest the underlying policy likely advanced elsewhere (the Senate version S. 647 was the vehicle the House pointed to), so the story of who ultimately won turns on that companion bill, not this one.

against.name: Senate (101st Congress)

against.what_they_did: The House took up the similar Senate bill S. 647 in place of this one, and no final enactment occurred before the Congress ended; no Senate floor vote on this bill is recorded in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (both Democratic and Republican original cosponsors, including the Republican ranking member) and passed the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition; the fight, if any, was not partisan but simply about which chamber's version of the bill would move.

industries.note: The bill's fraud-fighting provisions hit this group hardest: barred individuals could no longer work as 'promoters' or 'consultants' to evade SEC bans, and all penny stock brokers faced mandatory risk disclosures, commission disclosure, monthly customer statements, and participation in a transparent quotation system. These are the actors the bill explicitly targets as the source of 'overwhelming' fraud in the market.

Larger, legitimate firms would face new administrative enforcement powers the SEC could use against them (fines, stop orders, officer bans) but would also gain from a more credible market. Smaller firms focused on penny stocks would bear proportionally heavier compliance costs.

The bill targets companies that raise public money with no business plan, requiring special disclosure rules and possible rescission rights for their shareholders - a direct curb on a shell-company fundraising model.

Retail investors, the intended beneficiaries, get more information, a hotline to check broker disciplinary records, and recourse through disgorgement - protections that reduce the information advantage brokers had over them.
